questions.q: Per Compound's own published governance lifecycle diagram shown in this lesson, what stage comes immediately after a proposal succeeds and before it executes?
options: Immediate execution with no delay
A second, separate vote
Queued in the Timelock (a delay period)
Automatic cancellation
questions.explain: Compound's diagram shows Succeeded -> Queued (Timelock, 2 days) -> Executed -- a delay sits between a vote passing and the change actually applying.

questions.q: What does the quorum check verify, separately from the majority check?
options: That enough total voting power participated, regardless of how the votes split
That more than half of the votes cast were in favor
That the proposer has enough tokens to propose
That the timelock delay has expired
questions.explain: Quorum checks total participation (total_votes_cast >= quorum_threshold); majority separately checks the For/Against split.

questions.q: With quorum = 400,000, votes cast = 450,000, for_votes = 300,000, and against_votes = 150,000, does this proposal pass both checks?
options: No -- quorum fails
No -- majority fails
It's impossible to tell from this information
questions.explain: 450,000 total votes clears the 400,000 quorum, and 300,000/450,000 = 66.7%, which clears the 50% majority threshold.

questions.q: Why does Aave's governance architecture split proposal/governance logic on a Core network from vote casting on separate voting networks?
options: Because Ethereum cannot process any governance votes at all
To let large numbers of token holders vote cheaply on lower-fee chains without weakening where actual governance power resides
To prevent any proposals from ever being created
Voting networks have nothing to do with cost -- it's purely for marketing
questions.explain: The lesson explains this splits cheap vote casting from the Core network where governance power and proposals actually live, balancing cost and security.

questions.q: Why does quorum exist as a separate check from majority, per this lesson?
options: To stop a small, motivated minority from passing changes that the broader token-holder base never weighed in on
To make voting slower for no functional reason
To guarantee every proposal fails
Quorum and majority check exactly the same thing
questions.explain: A lopsided For/Against split means little if only a tiny fraction of eligible voting power actually participated -- quorum specifically guards against that.
